questions.question: What is resonance? Draw resonance structures of ozone and benzene.
questions.solution:
**Resonance:** When a single Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule, multiple structures (resonance contributors) are needed.

**Ozone (O₃):** O=O-O ↔ O-O=O (two equivalent structures)
**Benzene (C₆H₆):** Two Kekulé structures with alternating double bonds — actual structure is a resonance hybrid with equal C-C bond lengths.
questions.knowledgeNote: Resonance stabilization energy of benzene ≈ 152 kJ/mol — explains its unusual stability.
questions.answer: **Resonance:** the representation of a single real molecule by two or more Lewis structures (**contributing structures**) that differ only in π-electron/lone-pair placement — nuclei never move. The real molecule is the **resonance hybrid**, more stable (by the resonance energy) than any single structure. **Ozone, O₃:** two structures — O=O–O (with a positive charge on the singly-bonded terminal O) and ⁻O–O=O (mirror image); the hybrid has two **equal O–O bonds of 128 pm**, between single (148 pm) and double (121 pm) lengths, and a bent shape (≈117°). **Benzene, C₆H₆:** the two **Kekulé structures** with three alternating C=C bonds, related by shifting the π bonds one position around the ring; the hybrid has **six equal C–C bonds of 139 pm** and the ~152 kJ/mol resonance energy that makes it aromatic. **Deep point:** the measured bond lengths are the experiment's verdict on resonance — 128 pm and 139 pm are exactly the numbers 'between' predicts, and no single drawn structure could give them.
